documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
68M here to establish. Previous PCP retired; wife found us through a neighbor. Came in on his portable tank, 2 L.

Lungs: told he has COPD several years back, on continuous O2 2 L by concentrator at home since about 2017, portable for outings. Uses tiotropium every morning and salmeterol twice a day, nebulized albuterol a couple of times a week, more in winter. Gets winded with a flight of stairs, gets the mail fine. No recent steroid bursts that he recalls.

Liver: alcohol-related cirrhosis found on an ultrasound in 2018. Has not had a drink since January 2019. Sees an outside hepatology group twice a year for ultrasound and AFP. Says he was told there were no varices on a scope. Never had fluid or confusion.

BP and sugar: on lisinopril 20, HCTZ 25 and metformin 1000 bid for years. Does not check sugars at home.

C. diff 2019 - hospitalized about a week at an outside hospital, "the worst I've ever felt." No recurrence.

Smoking about 45 pack-years, quit 2014, went back to it for a few months in 2019 and stopped again. Alcohol as above, 4-6 drinks a day for decades before quitting. Retired construction foreman. Married, wife Ingrid.
FHx: father COPD and lung cancer. Mother T2DM. Brother cirrhosis.
PSH: none. NKDA.

Exam: thin, pleasant, mildly dyspneic after walking from the lot, speaking full sentences. BP and SpO2 as charted, on 2 L. No scleral icterus. Distant breath sounds, no wheeze. RRR, no murmur. Abdomen soft, nontender, no ascites appreciated. No asterixis. No edema.

A/P
1. COPD with chronic hypoxemic resp failure on 2 L - continue current inhalers and O2. Will take over DME orders once records are in.
2. Alcoholic cirrhosis, compensated, abstinent - continue hepatology surveillance. Check hep B status for vaccination; will need hep A/B.
3. HTN - at goal. Continue lisinopril/HCTZ.
4. T2DM - A1c today.
5. Hx severe C. diff - noted. Avoid unnecessary antibiotics.
6. Screening: HCV, HIV today. Asking for prior colonoscopy report.

Labs today. Records request sent. RTC 3 months.

documents.title: Pulmonology Consultation
documents.author: pulmonology
documents.body:
Outside pulmonology consultation, date of service 08/11/2021.
Referred by primary care for progressive breathlessness.

History: About six months of steadily increasing shortness of breath with exertion and a dry, nonproductive cough. He has had no fevers, no chest pain and no recent travel. Long-standing COPD on 2 L continuous oxygen, tiotropium and salmeterol, albuterol by nebulizer as needed. Former smoker, around 45 pack-years, quit 2014. Former heavy alcohol use, abstinent since 2019, with compensated cirrhosis. Retired construction foreman; no known asbestos or silica exposure beyond the usual job-site dust. Father had COPD and lung cancer.
Medications: as listed by primary care, plus lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide and metformin. Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: Digital clubbing. Fine inspiratory crackles at both lung bases. No wheeze. Heart regular, no edema.

Data: HRCT shows reticulation with honeycombing at the bases and in a subpleural distribution, with no embolism or acute process. Full PFTs show reduced lung volumes (TLC, FRC and RV all decreased) with preserved FEV1 and FVC and a raised FEV1/FVC ratio; DLCO is reduced.

Impression:
1. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. The CT pattern is typical, there is no clear exposure or connective tissue history, and the physiology is restrictive. In my view the fibrosis now dominates his lung mechanics, which is why the obstruction expected from his COPD is not evident on this study.
2. COPD with chronic hypoxemic respiratory failure, on oxygen.

Plan:
- Antifibrotic therapy (nintedanib or pirfenidone) discussed. Both carry hepatic risk and are not advised with his cirrhosis; we agreed not to start either for now.
- Continue oxygen 2 L and current inhalers.
- Repeat HRCT in about one year; follow-up here every 6 months.
- Vaccinations per primary care.

Pulmonology

Outside gastroenterology consultation, seen 01/27/2022, at the request of his primary care physician.

Reason: dysphagia.

HPI: Half a year of difficulty swallowing, mostly with solid food. Occasionally brings back undigested food, more often when lying flat. Describes something like a lump in the throat; his wife notes bad breath. Liquids pass. He has IPF diagnosed by pulmonology last summer, COPD on 2 L oxygen, and compensated alcohol-related cirrhosis followed by our hepatology colleagues.

Meds: tiotropium, salmeterol, albuterol nebs PRN, home O2 2 L, lisinopril 20, HCTZ 25, metformin 1000 bid. NKDA.

Exam: No neck mass on palpation. Cranial nerves and the rest of the neurological exam normal.

Barium esophagram (performed with this visit): posterior outpouching of the esophagus arising just above the upper esophageal sphincter, consistent with a Zenker diverticulum. Remainder of the esophagus passes contrast normally.

Assessment: Zenker diverticulum, symptomatic.

Plan: We discussed flexible endoscopic septotomy versus surgical options. Given his lung disease and oxygen requirement, he prefers to avoid sedation and a procedure for now, which is reasonable while he is maintaining his weight. Small bites, chew thoroughly, follow solids with liquids, stay upright for an hour after meals and avoid eating late. Return if he loses weight, has choking spells or recurrent chest infections.

documents.title: Microwave Ablation - Interventional Radiology
documents.author: interventional radiology
documents.body:
Outside interventional radiology procedure report, 03/09/2023.
Procedure: CT- and ultrasound-guided percutaneous microwave ablation, segment VI hepatocellular carcinoma (2.1 cm).
Anesthesia: general anesthesia with anesthesiology, chosen after discussion with pulmonology; extubated in the procedure suite, back on 2 L by recovery.
Technique: single antenna placed through a right intercostal approach; one ablation cycle covering the lesion with a 5 to 10 mm margin. Track ablated on withdrawal.
Post-ablation imaging: ablation zone encompasses the target; no hemorrhage or pneumothorax.
Complications: none. Discharged home the same evening.
Follow-up: multiphase MRI and AFP in about 3 months. NKDA.

reports.conclusion: Left lung re-expanded after chest tube. Small residual apical pneumothorax.

documents.title: Emergency Department Note
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Outside regional hospital ED, 02/02/2026.
CC: sudden breathlessness and left chest pain after a coughing fit.
HPI: 73-year-old man with COPD with chronic respiratory failure and IPF, on 2 L home oxygen and nebulizer, ICU stay last February for acute-on-chronic respiratory failure. This afternoon after a bout of coughing he felt a sudden sharp pain on the left side of his chest and could not catch his breath. Brought by his wife.
NKDA. Home meds per list.
Vitals: BP 145/90, HR 122, RR 28, SpO2 86% on room air.
Exam: anxious, tachypneic, tachycardic. Breath sounds diminished over the left chest without wheeze; hyperresonant to percussion on the left. Remainder of the exam unremarkable.
Portable CXR obtained at once: large left pneumothorax with rightward mediastinal shift.
Course: tension pneumothorax - needle decompression left second intercostal space, midclavicular line, with a rush of air and prompt improvement in heart rate and saturation; left chest tube then placed in the fifth intercostal space, anterior axillary line, under local anesthesia. Repeat film: lung re-expanded, small apical residual. SpO2 93% on 4 L.
Disposition: ICU for monitoring.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
Outside regional hospital. Admitted 02/02/2026, discharged 02/06/2026.
Diagnosis: left tension pneumothorax, secondary spontaneous, in a patient with COPD and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
Course: Needle decompression and left chest tube in the ED. Two days in the ICU, weaned back to 2 L. Small air leak resolved by day 3; tube placed to water seal then removed on hospital day 4 with no recurrence on follow-up film. Pain controlled. Thoracic surgery reviewed; no pleurodesis at this time.
Discharge medications: unchanged home regimen - oxygen 2 L continuous, tiotropium, salmeterol, albuterol nebs as needed, lisinopril 20, HCTZ 25, metformin 1000 twice daily.
Advice: no air travel until cleared by pulmonology; return for any sudden breathlessness or chest pain.
Allergies: NKDA.
Follow-up: PCP within one week; pulmonology in 6 to 8 weeks with chest x-ray.

documents.title: Post-Hospital Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
TCM. Tension pneumothorax on the left 2/2 after a coughing spell - needle decompression and chest tube in the ED, ICU 2 nights, tube out day 4, home 2/6. Records reviewed.
Now: chest tube site sore, improving. Breathing back to his usual on 2 L. No new sudden pain. Shaken by it. Wife did not leave his side.
Exam: sat as charted on 2 L. Left chest tube site clean and dry, sutured, no drainage. Breath sounds present both sides, basal crackles as before. Heart regular.
A/P: Left tension pneumothorax - resolved, clinically re-expanded. Suture out with nurse next week. Pulm f/u with CXR in April. Reviewed: call 911 for sudden chest pain or breathlessness. RTC May.
